question: At what hour did the battle (the infantry attack) begin?
reading_a: About 13:00, after half an hour's cannonade from about 12:30
reading_b: About 13:30
evidence_for:
S144 pp. 84, 87, 153: lead elements "around 1230", the line formed "around 1300", "1300—British advance on first line", "1315—First line breaks".
S143 Saumarez, in S138 p. 47: "About one o'clock the action commenced."
S138 p. 42: the cannonade "began some time just after noon and went on for at least a half hour".
evidence_against:
S139: "about half an hour past one in the afternoon" (in S144 p. 119), for "an action which lasted an hour and a half" (in S138 p. 47).
S140, in S138 p. 47: the "battle began about twelve o'clock, lasted about two hours" (he may count from the cannonade).
S141, in S138 p. 43: "About ten in the forenoon" (Hatch: much too early).
S144 p. ix (list of maps): Map 16, "The first line deployment, 1300–1330"; Map 17, "The first line breaks, 1330".
adopted_because: The staff ride's clock, which Saumarez and Hatch support, and which lies between Greene's hour and Cornwallis's. Every row keeps half an hour either side.
next_step: Read Babits and Howard on the timing. The staff ride's map titles (1330 for the break) and its text (1315) differ by a quarter of an hour.

question: At what hour were the morning fights near New Garden?
reading_a: About 08:15 to 10:00
reading_b: From about sunrise: 06:30 to 07:30
evidence_for:
S143 Seymour, in S138 pp. 23-24: "This action began about nine o'clock in the morning and continued about the space of an hour and a half."
S143 Houston, in S138 p. 33: "about ten o'clock ... we heard our light infantry and cavalry ... begin firing".
S143 orderly book, in S138 p. 22: the army to march "precisely At half past five"; S142: the picket met after "seven miles", about three hours' march for foot.
S144 p. 74: Lee "broke contact" at 1000.
evidence_against:
S141, in S138 p. 25: at the meeting house "The sun had just risen above the trees".
S144 pp. 72-73: the lane "around 0700", the second fight "around 0900", the third "around 1000".
S144 p. 153: "0300—Cornwallis begins movement", "0400-0500—Dragoon skirmishes at New Garden Meeting House".
adopted_because: Two journals kept at the time give nine and ten; the order to march at 05:30 makes a fight seven miles on before 07:30 unlikely for the infantry. Lee wrote thirty years later. The rows keep from 06:30.
next_step: Read Babits and Howard, and Newsome's edition of the orderly book, for the hour of the march.

question: When did Greene's army form its three lines?
reading_a: From about 10:00, when the firing was heard
reading_b: About 06:00
evidence_for:

question: Which North Carolina brigade stood north of the road in the first line?
reading_a: Eaton north, Butler south
reading_b: Butler north, Eaton south
evidence_for:
S138 p. 34: "Eaton's brigade ... was north of, with its left resting on, the New Garden Road. Butler's brigade ... had a like deployment on the south side", citing Caruthers (1856), p. 141, and his plans 2 and 3.
S144 Map 16, p. 89: EATON labelled north of the road, BUTLER south.
S144 p. 93: Butler's brigade against Leslie's 71st and von Bose, who were south of the road.
evidence_against:
S144 p. 87: "Running to the north in order from left to right was Brigadier General John Butler's North Carolina militia brigade ... Running to the south in order was Colonel Thomas Eaton's".
S144 p. 90: "Eaton's North Carolina brigade broke" with "Lee's Corps of Observation on Eaton's left flank".
adopted_because: Hatch gives his authority, and the staff ride's own map and one of its stands agree with him against its other text. Babits and Howard, whom the staff ride follows, have not been read (SR-19): this is the first point to settle from them.
next_step: Read Babits and Howard (candidate SC-SOU10). If they put Butler north on the pension evidence, swap the two brigades.

question: Where did the third line stand?
reading_a: On the high ground between the vale and Hunting (Richland) Creek, west of the courthouse
reading_b: About 400 yards further west, in the field between today's Tour Stops 5 and 7 (Schenck)
evidence_for:
S138 pp. 37-38, 73 and plans 2 to 5: "just west and across Hunting Creek from the courthouse", all north of the road.
S145 p. 4: "the third line actually stood about 400 yards east of its previously interpreted position, i.e., the monument-marked field located between Tour Stops 5 and 7".
S144 p. 104: "about 300 meters east of this location, on a ridgeline overlooking Richland Creek", citing Babits and Howard, p. 238; p. xx: the old marker "incorrectly identifies the area as the American third line"; later scholarship puts it "about 400 meters uphill to the east-northeast".
evidence_against:
S145 p. 22: Schenck in the 1880s "fixed the location of the third line west of Hunting Creek, maintaining that its left flank occupied the elevation at present-day Tour Stop 7"; accepted for a century.
S145 p. 22: archeologists surveyed the revised location in 1995 "and did not uncover any military material".
adopted_because: Three studies from 1971 to 2021 agree. Note the names: Hatch's "Hunting Creek" is the stream the USGS calls Richland Creek; the park today gives the name to the branch Hatch calls the vale.
next_step: Read the landscape report's maps and the 1995 survey report; fit the park's own line.

question: How strong was Greene's army?
reading_a: About 4,400
reading_b: Over 5,600
evidence_for:
S138 pp. 127-129: Continentals 1,700, militia 2,200, riflemen and volunteers 500; Gordon and F. V. Greene 4,444, Ward 4,463, Carrington 4,404; Lee's field return 4,449.
S144 p. 151: "~4,400 with 4,000 engaged".
S85 p. 98: "1,500 continentals and 3,000 militia".
evidence_against:
S138 p. 128: Schenck (1889) 5,668, "probably under the true figure"; Hatch thinks it inflated.
S139, in S138 p. 21 n. 1: Cornwallis heard "nine or ten thousand", and wrote of 5,000 to 7,000.
adopted_because: The returns and every study since agree within a hundred.

question: Did Cornwallis have his guns fire into his own Guards?
reading_a: Yes: grapeshot into the melee, friend and foe
reading_b: The guns fired to check the American pursuit; Guardsmen were hit, but not by design
evidence_for:
S141, in S138 p. 82: Cornwallis "ordered his artillery to fire, sacrificing the fugitives to check the pursuit".
S138 p. 82: "though it would be into both friend and foe alike and over the objection of the Guards commander, O'Hara".
evidence_against:
S139: "The enemy's cavalry was soon repulsed by a well-directed fire from two three pounders": no word of firing on his own men.
S144 p. 107: the grapeshot "apparently caused casualties among the guardsmen, giving rise to the assertion that Cornwallis cold-bloodedly ordered indiscriminate firing into the melee" (its note 83: Babits and Howard, pp. 161-62, "thoroughly debunks the theory").
adopted_because: The newer study rejects the story on Babits and Howard's authority (not read here); Lee was in the south and did not see it. The event text says only that the guns fired grapeshot into the melee and checked the Americans.
next_step: Read Babits and Howard, pp. 161-62.

question: How far apart were the three lines?
reading_a: About 300 yards, then about 500
reading_b: 400 metres (437 yards), then 650 to 750 metres
evidence_for: S138 pp. 36-38: the second line "some 300 yards behind the first", the third "some 500 yards behind the second"; Schenck measured the second and third "at least five hundred and fifty (550) yards apart".
evidence_against:
S140: "about three hundred yards ... about four hundred yards".
S142: 400 and "near six hundred yards".
S144 pp. 87, 95, 97: "About 437 yards (400 meters)"; the third line 650 m north-east of Lawson and 750 m east-north-east of Stevens.
adopted_because: The lines are drawn where Hatch's plans put them: on the ground about 430 m apart at the road, then about 620 m. That is nearer the staff ride's figures than Hatch's own text.

question: Where were the morning fights, and where was Lee posted?
reading_a: At three junctions of New Garden Road: Hobbs Road ("the lane"), West Friendly Avenue (the meeting house) and Ballinger Road (the cross road)
reading_b: All nearer the meeting house, four miles from the courthouse
evidence_for:
S144 pp. 72-74 and Map 13: the lane 1.8 miles north-east of the meeting house, the second fight at the West Friendly Avenue junction, the third at "the Ballenger and Great Salisbury Cross Roads" 0.6 mile north.
S139: "About four miles from Guildford our advanced guard ... fell in with a corps of the enemy".
evidence_against:
S141, in S138 pp. 23-25: Lee was posted "within two or three miles of the court-house", met Heard "About two miles out" (Hatch's words), fell back, charged in the lane, then followed to the meeting house.
S141 (in S144 p. 74): the meeting house "not more than six miles from our head-quarters".
S144 p. 73 has Lee's corps at New Garden from 14 March.
adopted_because: The staff ride names places that can be found on the map, and Lee's distances fit a lane between his post and the meeting house. Every morning row is rated low, good to 400 m at best.
next_step: Read Babits and Howard's chapter on New Garden; find the old meeting house site (Hatch, p. 25 n. 13: foundation stones about 200 yards from the Guilford College campus).
